name: Honey and burnt salt tooth whitening in vinegar

image.caption: Honey and burnt salt tooth whitening in vinegar

lead: Honey and burnt salt with a little vinegar is a historical tooth-cleaning recipe, attributed to the 14th-century surgeon Guy de Chauliac. The aim was a cleaner, whiter-looking set of teeth, which has long been tied to attractiveness and status.

The burnt salt acts as a mild grit, the honey binds it into a paste, and the vinegar adds acidity. Wikipedia describes it among the earliest recorded whitening methods; no modern clinical trial of the mixture is known.

paras: Historically the paste was rubbed gently on the teeth. It is now mostly a curiosity of dental history, and modern whitening relies on peroxide-based products and professional cleaning.
Dental sources describe acid and abrasives as capable of wearing away enamel, and enamel does not regrow. Acid erosion is listed as a reason to avoid some whitening procedures.

angle.text: The recipe was used to scrub surface discolouration from teeth so they look cleaner and whiter. Its effect is described in historical accounts rather than measured in trials.

lead: Honey and burnt salt tooth whitening in vinegar is a folk recipe for cleaning the teeth. Wikipedia's article on tooth whitening quotes the medieval surgeon Guy de Chauliac as advising that the teeth be cleaned gently with honey and burnt salt to which some vinegar has been added [1].

People used such mixtures to remove stains and make the teeth look brighter. Pale, even teeth have been associated with beauty and wealth since antiquity, and Roman dentists are reported to have used other home preparations for the same purpose [1].
No modern clinical studies of this specific recipe are known. Dental literature on whitening generally notes that very acidic products and highly abrasive pastes can damage dental tissue [1].

paras: The mixture combines three household ingredients: honey as a binder, burnt salt as a fine abrasive, and vinegar as a mild acid. Wikipedia cites it as a recommendation of Guy de Chauliac, a medieval surgeon [1].

It belongs to a long line of pre-modern whitening practices that includes Roman preparations and Ayurvedic oil pulling. In the late 17th century barbers filed teeth and applied acid, which whitened them but left them eroded and more prone to decay [1]. Chemical bleaching agents such as oxalic acid were proposed in 1877, and peroxide gels followed in the mid-20th century [1].

Dentistry sources state that abrasive whitening toothpastes with excessive abrasivity are harmful to dental tissue, and that acid erosion is a contraindication for whitening treatments [1]. These statements are general; they do not describe tests of this particular recipe.
